Choosing the Right Mental Health Profess:
Frequently Asked Questions About Seeing a Psychiatrist
Seeking help for your mental health is an important step, and it's common to wonder whether you should see a psychiatrist, psychologist, therapist, or another healthcare professional. Understanding the differences can help you choose the care that's right for your needs.
________________________________________
What does a psychiatrist do?
A psychiatrist is a medical doctor (MD or DO) who specializes in diagnosing, treating, and preventing mental health conditions.
Because psychiatrists complete medical school followed by specialized residency training in psychiatry, they understand the complex relationship between emotional health, brain function, medications, hormones, chronic medical conditions, and overall physical health.
Psychiatrists can:
•	Diagnose mental health conditions
•	Prescribe medications when appropriate
•	Monitor medication safety and effectiveness
•	Provide supportive psychotherapy during visits
•	Order laboratory tests when clinically indicated
•	Coordinate care with therapists and other physicians
At Paramount Psychiatry, we combine medical expertise with compassionate, patient-centered care to create individualized treatment plans that address the whole person.
________________________________________
What is the difference between a psychiatrist and a psychologist?
Although psychiatrists and psychologists both care for people with mental health conditions, their training and roles are different.
A psychiatrist is a physician who specializes in mental health and can prescribe medication, diagnose psychiatric conditions, and evaluate how medical conditions may be affecting emotional well-being.
A psychologist typically holds a doctoral degree in psychology and specializes in psychological testing and psychotherapy but generally does not prescribe medication in most states.
Many patients benefit from seeing both a psychiatrist and a psychologist. Psychotherapy and medication management often complement one another and can provide the best long-term outcomes.
________________________________________
What is the difference between a psychiatrist and a therapist?
Therapists—including licensed clinical social workers (LCSWs), licensed professional counselors (LPCs), licensed marriage and family therapists (LMFTs), and psychologists—primarily provide psychotherapy to help patients develop coping skills, improve relationships, process emotions, and manage life challenges.
Psychiatrists focus on diagnosing mental health conditions, evaluating medical contributors to emotional symptoms, prescribing medications when appropriate, and overseeing psychiatric treatment.
At Paramount Psychiatry, we believe psychiatric care and psychotherapy often work best together. When appropriate, we collaborate closely with therapists to provide coordinated, comprehensive care.
________________________________________
When should I consider seeing a psychiatrist?
Many people wonder whether their symptoms are "serious enough" to seek psychiatric care. The truth is that you don't need to wait until you're in crisis.
You may benefit from seeing a psychiatrist if you are experiencing:
•	Persistent anxiety or excessive worry
•	Depression or loss of interest in activities
•	Difficulty concentrating or symptoms of ADHD
•	Panic attacks
•	Mood swings
•	Difficulty sleeping
•	Obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors
•	Trauma-related symptoms
•	Significant stress or burnout
•	Memory or cognitive concerns
•	Emotional changes related to hormonal or medical conditions
If your symptoms are interfering with work, school, relationships, daily functioning, or your quality of life, a psychiatric evaluation can help identify the cause and explore treatment options.
________________________________________
Do I need medication to see a psychiatrist?
No.
Many people assume psychiatrists only prescribe medication, but that is a common misconception.
At Paramount Psychiatry, every patient receives an individualized evaluation. Medication may be recommended when appropriate, but it is never the only option and is never prescribed simply because you scheduled an appointment.
Depending on your needs, your treatment plan may include education, supportive psychotherapy, lifestyle modifications, sleep optimization, stress management strategies, referrals for ongoing therapy, medication management, or a combination of these approaches.
Treatment decisions are always made collaboratively.
________________________________________
Can a psychiatrist diagnose ADHD?
Yes.
Psychiatrists are qualified to evaluate, diagnose, and treat Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in adolescents and adults.
An ADHD evaluation involves much more than completing a checklist. During your appointment, we review your current symptoms, developmental history, educational and work experiences, medical history, previous treatments, and other factors that may affect attention and concentration.
Because symptoms such as anxiety, depression, sleep disorders, thyroid disease, and other medical conditions can sometimes resemble ADHD, a comprehensive evaluation is essential to ensure an accurate diagnosis.
________________________________________
Can a psychiatrist help even if I'm not sure what's wrong?
Absolutely.
You do not need to know your diagnosis before scheduling an appointment.
Many patients come to us with symptoms such as feeling overwhelmed, anxious, emotionally exhausted, having trouble sleeping, difficulty concentrating, or simply feeling "not like themselves."
One of the primary goals of a psychiatric evaluation is to understand what may be contributing to these symptoms and develop an individualized treatment plan based on your unique situation.
________________________________________
Can I see both a therapist and a psychiatrist?
Yes, and in many cases this combination provides the most comprehensive care.
Psychotherapy helps individuals develop coping strategies, improve relationships, process difficult emotions, and build long-term resilience.
Psychiatric care focuses on diagnosis, medication management when appropriate, and evaluating the medical and biological factors that may influence mental health.
With your permission, we are happy to collaborate with your therapist to ensure coordinated and consistent care.
________________________________________
Can my primary care doctor treat anxiety or depression instead of seeing a psychiatrist?
Primary care physicians play an important role in identifying and treating many common mental health conditions, and some patients do very well under their care.
However, a psychiatrist may be beneficial if:
•	Symptoms are persistent or worsening
•	Previous treatments have not been effective
•	You have experienced medication side effects
•	Your diagnosis is unclear
•	Multiple mental health conditions may be present
•	You require specialized medication management
•	Hormonal or medical conditions may be contributing to your symptoms
•	You would like a second opinion
Psychiatrists receive specialized training in diagnosing and treating complex mental health conditions and can provide more in-depth evaluations when needed.
________________________________________
Is it okay to seek a second opinion?
Absolutely.
Mental health conditions can be complex, and seeking a second opinion is a reasonable and sometimes helpful step.
Patients often seek a second opinion when:
•	They are uncertain about a previous diagnosis.
•	They have tried several medications without improvement.
•	They are experiencing unwanted side effects.
•	They would like to explore additional treatment options.
•	They simply want reassurance before making an important treatment decision.
Our goal is to provide an objective, thoughtful evaluation and help you understand your options so you can make informed decisions about your care.
________________________________________
Is seeing a psychiatrist a sign that something is seriously wrong?
Not at all.
Seeking psychiatric care is no different than seeing a cardiologist for heart health or an endocrinologist for diabetes or thyroid concerns. It is simply an opportunity to better understand your mental health and receive expert guidance.
Many people seek psychiatric care for relatively common concerns such as anxiety, stress, ADHD, insomnia, burnout, or life transitions. Others seek support during difficult periods such as pregnancy, menopause, grief, caregiving, or major career changes.
Reaching out for help is a sign of self-awareness and strength—not weakness.
________________________________________

Understanding Psychiatric Diagnosis & Tr:
Frequently Asked Questions About Psychiatric Evaluations, Diagnosis, and Treatment Planning
Mental health conditions are often more complex than they appear. Many different conditions can share similar symptoms, and emotional well-being is influenced by medical conditions, hormones, sleep, stress, genetics, and life experiences.
At Paramount Psychiatry, we believe that an accurate diagnosis is the foundation of effective treatment. Our goal is to understand the complete picture before making recommendations, ensuring that every treatment plan is thoughtful, individualized, and based on the best available evidence.
________________________________________
How do psychiatrists diagnose mental health conditions?
Psychiatric diagnosis is a comprehensive process—not simply a checklist of symptoms.
During your evaluation, Dr. Tandon carefully considers many factors, including your current symptoms, medical history, psychiatric history, family history, medications, lifestyle, sleep, work or school functioning, relationships, and any recent life changes.
She also evaluates whether medical conditions, medications, hormonal changes, or substance use may be contributing to your symptoms.
Rather than focusing on one symptom in isolation, psychiatric diagnosis looks at patterns over time and how those symptoms affect your daily life.
Our goal is to make the most accurate diagnosis possible so that treatment is tailored to your individual needs.
________________________________________
Why is a comprehensive psychiatric evaluation so important?
Many mental health conditions share similar symptoms.
For example, difficulty concentrating may be related to ADHD, anxiety, depression, sleep deprivation, thyroid disease, medication side effects, menopause, or another medical condition.
Similarly, irritability, fatigue, memory problems, or mood changes can have many different causes.
A comprehensive evaluation helps distinguish between these possibilities, reducing the risk of misdiagnosis and ensuring that treatment addresses the underlying cause—not just the symptoms.
Taking time to understand the whole person leads to more effective, personalized care.
________________________________________
Can mental health symptoms be caused by medical conditions?
Yes.
Physical health and mental health are closely connected.
Medical conditions such as thyroid disorders, diabetes, vitamin deficiencies, chronic pain, neurological disorders, hormonal changes, menopause, pregnancy, postpartum changes, and sleep disorders can all contribute to symptoms of anxiety, depression, poor concentration, irritability, fatigue, or memory changes.
That's why we take a whole-person approach to psychiatric care. When appropriate, we may recommend additional medical evaluation or collaborate with your primary care physician or specialists to ensure all contributing factors are addressed.
________________________________________
Can hormones affect my mental health?
Absolutely.
Hormonal changes can significantly influence mood, anxiety, sleep, energy, concentration, and emotional well-being.
Many individuals experience psychiatric symptoms related to:
•	Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)
•	Pregnancy
•	Postpartum changes
•	Perimenopause
•	Menopause
•	Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
•	Thyroid disorders
•	Other endocrine conditions
Because these conditions can overlap with depression or anxiety, understanding the role of hormones is an important part of developing an effective treatment plan.
________________________________________
Why might laboratory testing be recommended?
Psychiatric symptoms sometimes have underlying medical causes.
Depending on your symptoms, medical history, and current medications, Dr. Tandon may recommend laboratory testing or ask you to follow up with your primary care physician.
Laboratory testing can help identify conditions such as thyroid disorders, vitamin deficiencies, metabolic concerns, or other medical issues that may be contributing to emotional or cognitive symptoms.
Certain psychiatric medications may also require routine laboratory monitoring to ensure they remain safe and effective.
________________________________________
Can more than one mental health condition occur at the same time?
Yes.
It's very common for individuals to experience more than one mental health condition simultaneously.
For example:
•	ADHD may occur alongside anxiety or depression.
•	Anxiety and depression frequently occur together.
•	Trauma may contribute to sleep difficulties, mood changes, and anxiety.
•	Hormonal changes may worsen existing mental health conditions.
Identifying all contributing conditions helps create a treatment plan that addresses the complete picture rather than focusing on only one diagnosis.
________________________________________
What if my symptoms don't fit neatly into one diagnosis?
Not every person fits perfectly into a single diagnostic category.
Mental health exists on a spectrum, and symptoms often evolve over time.
Some individuals experience overlapping symptoms or may be in the early stages of a condition where additional observation is helpful before making a definitive diagnosis.
Rather than rushing to assign a label, we focus on understanding your experiences and developing a treatment plan that addresses your current needs while continuing to reassess as more information becomes available.
________________________________________
Can a psychiatric diagnosis change over time?
Yes.
Mental health is dynamic, and diagnoses may change as symptoms evolve, new information becomes available, or life circumstances change.
This does not necessarily mean a previous diagnosis was "wrong." Instead, it reflects the fact that psychiatric conditions can develop gradually, overlap with other conditions, or present differently over time.
Regular follow-up appointments allow us to monitor your progress and adjust your diagnosis or treatment plan when appropriate.
________________________________________
What if I was previously diagnosed but I'm not sure it was accurate?

No.

________________________________________
How do you decide whether medication is appropriate?
Medication decisions are individualized and based on many factors.
During your evaluation, Dr. Tandon considers:
•	Your symptoms
•	Medical history
•	Previous psychiatric treatment
•	Current medications

•	Sleep patterns

Some individuals improve with psychotherapy, lifestyle changes, improved sleep, stress reduction, or treatment of underlying medical conditions. Others benefit most from combining medication with therapy and healthy lifestyle habits.
At Paramount Psychiatry, treatment is always personalized, and medication is recommended only when it is likely to provide meaningful benefit.
________________________________________
Will medication change my personality?
This is one of the most common concerns we hear, and the answer is generally no.
The purpose of psychiatric medication is not to change who you are—it is to help reduce symptoms that may be preventing you from feeling like yourself.
When medication is working well, many patients report that they feel more emotionally balanced, better able to concentrate, sleep more consistently, and enjoy daily life again. They often describe feeling more like themselves, not less.
If you ever feel emotionally "numb," unlike yourself, or uncomfortable with how a medication affects you, we encourage you to let us know. Your treatment plan can often be adjusted.
________________________________________
How long does it take psychiatric medications to work?
The timeline depends on the medication being prescribed.
Many medications used to treat depression and anxiety begin working gradually over several weeks, while some medications used for ADHD or sleep may work much sooner.
It's important to continue taking medication exactly as prescribed and attend follow-up appointments so we can monitor your progress and make adjustments if necessary.
During treatment, we'll discuss what improvements to expect, how long they may take, and when to contact us if you have concerns.
________________________________________
Will I have side effects?
Like all medications, psychiatric medications can have side effects.
Fortunately, many side effects are mild, temporary, or manageable.
Before prescribing any medication, Dr. Tandon will discuss:
•	Why the medication is being recommended
•	Expected benefits
•	Possible side effects
•	Safety considerations
•	Potential medication interactions
•	Alternative treatment options
Our goal is to help you make informed decisions and ensure that any treatment plan is both safe and effective.
________________________________________
What if a medication doesn't work?
Finding the right medication sometimes takes time.
Every person's brain chemistry, genetics, medical history, and life circumstances are different, which means people respond differently to medications.
If a medication is not providing adequate benefit or is causing unwanted side effects, we will review your progress together and discuss appropriate adjustments.
Treatment is an ongoing process, and our goal is to find the safest and most effective approach for you.
________________________________________
Can I stop taking my medication once I feel better?
It depends.
Some medications can be stopped after symptoms improve, while others may be recommended for longer periods to reduce the risk of symptoms returning.
You should never stop psychiatric medication abruptly without first speaking with your psychiatrist, as doing so may cause withdrawal symptoms or increase the risk of relapse.
If medication is no longer needed, we'll work together to develop a safe plan for gradually reducing or discontinuing treatment when appropriate.
________________________________________
How often will my medications be reviewed?
Medication management is an ongoing process.
At each follow-up appointment, we'll discuss:
•	How well your medication is working
•	Any side effects
•	Changes in your symptoms
•	Sleep
•	Appetite
•	Stress levels
•	Medical changes
•	Any concerns or questions you may have
Adjustments are made only when clinically appropriate and with your input.
________________________________________
Do you prescribe controlled medications?
Yes—when they are medically appropriate.
Certain medications used to treat conditions such as ADHD or severe anxiety are classified as controlled substances and are regulated by both federal and state law.
When these medications are indicated, prescribing is based on a comprehensive psychiatric evaluation, careful clinical judgment, and all applicable legal and regulatory requirements.
Patient safety is always our highest priority.
________________________________________
Are controlled substances prescribed at every visit?
No.
Controlled medications are prescribed only when clinically appropriate.
Whenever possible, we aim to use the safest and most effective treatment options. In some cases, non-controlled medications or non-medication approaches may be recommended instead.
If a controlled medication is part of your treatment plan, ongoing monitoring and regular follow-up appointments are required to ensure continued safety and effectiveness.
________________________________________
Why do controlled medications require additional monitoring?
Controlled substances have important medical benefits but also require careful oversight.
Depending on the medication and current regulations, patients may be required to:
•	Attend regular follow-up appointments
•	Participate in periodic in-person visits
•	Use a single pharmacy whenever possible
•	Complete additional documentation
•	Undergo laboratory testing or other monitoring when clinically indicated
•	Have Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) records reviewed, as required by law
These measures help ensure medications are prescribed safely and responsibly.
________________________________________
Do you provide medication refills between appointments?
Yes, when appropriate.
Patients should request refills several business days before their medication runs out.
Refills are generally provided for patients who are actively participating in treatment and attending recommended follow-up appointments.
For many medications, prescriptions may be written for up to 90 days, depending on the medication, insurance requirements, and clinical judgment.
________________________________________
Can I request an early refill?
Early refill requests are reviewed individually but generally cannot be guaranteed.
Certain medications—particularly controlled substances—are subject to strict state and federal regulations regarding refill timing.
If you believe you have an exceptional circumstance, please contact our office as soon as possible so we can review your situation.
________________________________________
What if I lose my prescription or medication?
Lost, stolen, damaged, or misplaced medications—especially controlled substances—cannot routinely be replaced.
If this occurs, please notify our office promptly. Replacement requests will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis and in accordance with applicable laws, clinical judgment, and practice policies.
________________________________________
Can psychiatric medications interact with my other medications?
Yes.
This is one of the reasons a comprehensive medication review is such an important part of your psychiatric evaluation.
Before prescribing medication, Dr. Tandon carefully reviews your current medications, supplements, allergies, and medical history to reduce the risk of interactions.
Please let us know whenever another healthcare provider starts, stops, or changes any medication, including over-the-counter medicines and herbal supplements.
________________________________________
What if I'm pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding?
If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, please let us know as early as possible.
Many psychiatric medications can be safely used during pregnancy and breastfeeding, while others may require adjustment or closer monitoring.
Treatment decisions during pregnancy are highly individualized and involve carefully balancing the benefits of treatment with potential risks to both parent and baby. We also work collaboratively with your obstetrician or other healthcare providers when appropriate.
________________________________________
Can psychiatric medications help with menopause, PMDD, or hormonal mood changes?
Yes.
Hormonal changes can significantly affect mood, anxiety, sleep, and emotional well-being.
Depending on your symptoms and overall health, treatment may include psychiatric medication, hormone-related discussions with your OB/GYN or endocrinologist, psychotherapy, lifestyle changes, or a combination of approaches.
Our goal is to develop a treatment plan that addresses the underlying contributors to your symptoms while supporting your overall health.
________________________________________
What if I prefer not to take medication?
That's completely okay.
Many patients come to us seeking guidance rather than a prescription.
If medication is not your preference, we'll discuss alternative treatment strategies whenever appropriate. These may include psychotherapy, stress management, sleep optimization, exercise, mindfulness, behavioral techniques, lifestyle modifications, or coordination with other healthcare professionals.
Our role is to provide expert recommendations—not pressure you into a treatment you are uncomfortable with.
________________________________________
What is your overall philosophy on medication management?
We believe medications should be prescribed thoughtfully, conservatively, and only when the potential benefits clearly outweigh the risks.
Every medication decision is individualized and made collaboratively with the patient. We strive to prescribe the lowest effective dose, monitor treatment carefully, minimize unnecessary medications, and regularly reassess whether each medication continues to support your goals.
Our ultimate objective is not simply symptom relief—it's helping you achieve better emotional health, improved daily functioning, and a higher quality of life while using the safest and most appropriate treatment plan possible.
Understanding Anxiety, Stress & Panic Di:
Frequently Asked Questions About Anxiety and Panic Disorders
Everyone experiences stress and worry from time to time. However, when anxiety becomes persistent, overwhelming, or begins interfering with your relationships, work, sleep, or daily life, it may be time to seek professional help.
At Paramount Psychiatry, we understand that anxiety can affect every aspect of your life. Whether you're experiencing constant worry, panic attacks, physical symptoms, or anxiety related to work, health, relationships, or major life transitions, our goal is to help you understand what's happening and develop a personalized treatment plan that helps you regain confidence and peace of mind.
________________________________________
What is anxiety?
Anxiety is your body's natural response to stress or perceived danger. In many situations, anxiety is helpful—it prepares us to respond to challenges, stay alert, and solve problems.
However, when anxiety becomes excessive, persistent, or difficult to control, it can begin to interfere with daily life. An anxiety disorder is more than occasional worry. It can affect your thoughts, emotions, physical health, relationships, sleep, work performance, and overall quality of life.
The good news is that anxiety disorders are among the most treatable mental health conditions, and many people experience significant improvement with the right care.
________________________________________
What's the difference between normal stress and an anxiety disorder?
Everyone experiences stress, especially during major life events such as starting a new job, preparing for an exam, caring for a loved one, or managing financial concerns.
Stress usually improves once the situation resolves.
An anxiety disorder is different. The worry may feel excessive, difficult to control, or continue even when there is no immediate threat. Anxiety may persist for months, affect multiple areas of life, and make everyday tasks feel overwhelming.
If anxiety is interfering with your ability to work, sleep, maintain relationships, or enjoy daily activities, a psychiatric evaluation can help determine whether you're experiencing an anxiety disorder and what treatment options may be appropriate.
________________________________________
What are the common symptoms of anxiety?
Anxiety affects both the mind and the body. Symptoms vary from person to person but often include:
Emotional symptoms:
•	Excessive worrying
•	Feeling overwhelmed
•	Restlessness
•	Irritability
•	Feeling on edge
•	Difficulty relaxing
•	Fear that something bad will happen
Physical symptoms:
•	Rapid heartbeat
•	Chest tightness
•	Shortness of breath
•	Sweating
•	Trembling
•	Muscle tension
•	Headaches
•	Dizziness
•	Stomach discomfort or nausea
•	Fatigue
Cognitive symptoms:
•	Racing thoughts
•	Difficulty concentrating
•	Forgetfulness
•	Feeling mentally exhausted
•	Constant overthinking
Not everyone experiences the same symptoms, which is why a comprehensive evaluation is important.
________________________________________
Can anxiety cause physical symptoms?
Yes.
Many people are surprised to learn that anxiety can produce very real physical symptoms.
Because anxiety activates the body's "fight-or-flight" response, it can affect nearly every organ system. Some individuals experience chest discomfort, heart palpitations, dizziness, gastrointestinal problems, muscle pain, headaches, tingling sensations, or difficulty breathing.
These symptoms are real—not "all in your head."
However, it's also important to rule out underlying medical conditions that can produce similar symptoms. At Paramount Psychiatry, we consider both your mental and physical health when developing a diagnosis and treatment plan.
________________________________________
What is a panic attack?
A panic attack is a sudden episode of intense fear or discomfort that typically reaches its peak within minutes.
During a panic attack, people may experience:
•	A racing or pounding heart
•	Chest pain or tightness
•	Difficulty breathing
•	Sweating
•	Trembling
•	Dizziness
•	Feeling detached from reality
•	Fear of losing control
•	Fear of dying
Because panic attacks can feel similar to a heart attack, many people seek emergency medical care during their first episode.
Although panic attacks can be frightening, they are treatable, and effective treatments are available.
________________________________________
What's the difference between anxiety and a panic attack?
Anxiety usually develops gradually and may persist for hours, days, or even months. It often involves ongoing worry, muscle tension, restlessness, and difficulty concentrating.
A panic attack, on the other hand, is a sudden and intense surge of fear that develops rapidly and typically resolves within several minutes to an hour.
Some individuals experience panic attacks without ongoing anxiety, while others have both. Understanding the difference helps guide the most appropriate treatment approach.
________________________________________
What causes anxiety disorders?
There is rarely a single cause.
Anxiety often develops because of a combination of factors, including:
•	Genetics and family history
•	Brain chemistry
•	Personality traits
•	Chronic stress
•	Trauma or adverse life experiences
•	Medical conditions
•	Hormonal changes
•	Sleep deprivation
•	Certain medications or substances
Understanding what contributes to your anxiety helps us develop a treatment plan tailored to your specific needs.
________________________________________
Can anxiety affect sleep?
Absolutely.
Anxiety and sleep are closely connected.
Many people with anxiety have difficulty falling asleep because their minds feel constantly active. Others wake frequently during the night or wake up feeling unrefreshed despite spending enough time in bed.
Poor sleep can also worsen anxiety, creating a cycle that's difficult to break.
Improving sleep is often an important part of anxiety treatment.
________________________________________
Can anxiety affect my concentration and memory?
Yes.
When your brain is constantly focused on worry or perceived threats, it has fewer resources available for attention, memory, learning, and decision-making.
Many people with anxiety describe experiencing:
•	Brain fog
•	Difficulty focusing
•	Forgetfulness
•	Trouble completing tasks
•	Feeling mentally exhausted
These symptoms are common and often improve as anxiety becomes better controlled.
________________________________________
Can anxiety be mistaken for ADHD?
Yes.
Anxiety and ADHD can share symptoms such as difficulty concentrating, restlessness, racing thoughts, and trouble completing tasks.
However, the underlying causes are different, and treatment approaches may also differ.
One of the goals of a comprehensive psychiatric evaluation is to determine whether symptoms are related to anxiety, ADHD, both conditions, or another medical or psychological concern.
An accurate diagnosis is essential for developing the most effective treatment plan.
________________________________________
Can medical conditions cause anxiety?
Yes.
Several medical conditions can contribute to anxiety symptoms, including thyroid disorders, hormonal changes, heart conditions, respiratory illnesses, vitamin deficiencies, chronic pain, neurological disorders, and certain medications.
Because of this, Dr. Tandon considers both mental and physical health during every evaluation and may recommend additional medical evaluation or collaboration with your primary care physician when appropriate.
________________________________________
How are anxiety disorders diagnosed?
There is no single blood test or brain scan that diagnoses anxiety.
Diagnosis is based on a comprehensive psychiatric evaluation that includes your symptoms, medical history, psychiatric history, medications, family history, lifestyle, sleep, and the impact anxiety has on your daily life.
Our goal is not simply to identify symptoms but to understand the factors contributing to them so we can recommend the most appropriate treatment.
________________________________________
How are anxiety disorders treated?
Treatment depends on your symptoms, diagnosis, medical history, and personal preferences.
Your individualized treatment plan may include:
•	Education about anxiety
•	Medication management when appropriate
•	Supportive psychotherapy during visits
•	Referral for ongoing psychotherapy
•	Stress management techniques
•	Sleep optimization
•	Mindfulness and relaxation strategies
•	Lifestyle modifications
•	Coordination with other healthcare providers
No two treatment plans are exactly alike because no two patients experience anxiety in the same way.
________________________________________
Can anxiety be treated without medication?
Yes.
Many individuals benefit from psychotherapy, stress reduction techniques, mindfulness, improved sleep, regular physical activity, relaxation exercises, and healthy lifestyle changes.
Medication may be recommended for some patients, particularly when symptoms are more severe or significantly affecting daily functioning, but it is never the only treatment option.
Treatment decisions are always made collaboratively and based on your individual goals and preferences.
________________________________________
When is medication recommended for anxiety?
Medication may be recommended when anxiety is significantly interfering with your daily life, relationships, work, or overall well-being, or when symptoms have not improved with non-medication approaches alone.
If medication is appropriate, we'll discuss the potential benefits, possible side effects, expected timeline for improvement, and any alternative treatment options so you can make an informed decision.
________________________________________
Can anxiety disorders be cured?
Many people experience substantial improvement and lead full, productive lives with appropriate treatment.
Some individuals have temporary episodes of anxiety related to specific life circumstances, while others benefit from longer-term management strategies.
Rather than focusing solely on the word "cure," we focus on helping you reduce symptoms, build resilience, improve functioning, and develop the skills needed to manage anxiety effectively over time.
________________________________________
When should I seek professional help for anxiety?
You don't need to wait until anxiety becomes overwhelming.
Consider scheduling an evaluation if anxiety is:
•	Affecting your work or school performance
•	Interfering with relationships
•	Disrupting your sleep
•	Causing frequent physical symptoms
•	Preventing you from enjoying activities
•	Leading you to avoid situations or responsibilities
•	Persisting despite your own efforts to manage it
Early treatment often leads to better outcomes and may help prevent symptoms from becoming more severe.
________________________________________
What can I do today to help manage anxiety?
While professional treatment is important for many people, there are also practical steps you can take to support your mental well-being:
•	Maintain a regular sleep schedule
•	Stay physically active
•	Limit caffeine and alcohol if they worsen your symptoms
•	Practice mindfulness or deep breathing exercises
•	Spend time outdoors
•	Stay connected with supportive family and friends
•	Establish healthy daily routines
•	Take breaks from constant news and social media when needed
These strategies are not a substitute for professional care but can complement your treatment plan.
________________________________________
How can Paramount Psychiatry help?
At Paramount Psychiatry, we understand that anxiety looks different for every person.
Some patients experience constant worrying. Others struggle with panic attacks, physical symptoms, social anxiety, health anxiety, or anxiety related to major life transitions. Our role is to understand your unique experience—not simply assign a diagnosis.
Dr. Tandon takes the time to perform a comprehensive evaluation, identify the factors contributing to your symptoms, and develop a personalized treatment plan that reflects your goals, preferences, and overall health.
Our mission is to help you move beyond simply coping with anxiety so you can feel more confident, more resilient, and more fully engaged in your daily life.
Understanding Depression & Mood Disorder:
Frequently Asked Questions About Depression, Bipolar Disorder, and Other Mood Disorders
Everyone experiences periods of sadness, disappointment, or emotional stress. However, when changes in mood begin to interfere with daily life, relationships, work, or overall well-being, they may represent a treatable mental health condition rather than simply a difficult period in life.
At Paramount Psychiatry, we understand that mood disorders affect every person differently. Our goal is to understand not only your symptoms, but also the biological, psychological, hormonal, medical, and life circumstances contributing to those symptoms so we can develop a treatment plan that is personalized, evidence-based, and focused on helping you feel like yourself again.
________________________________________
What is depression?
Depression is a common medical condition that affects the way you think, feel, and function. It is much more than feeling sad or having a bad day.
People with depression often experience persistent feelings of sadness, emptiness, hopelessness, or loss of interest in activities they once enjoyed. Depression can also affect sleep, energy, concentration, appetite, motivation, and physical health.
Depression is not a sign of weakness or a personal failure. It is a treatable medical condition, and with appropriate care, many people experience significant improvement and return to living fulfilling, productive lives.
________________________________________
What are the common symptoms of depression?
Depression affects individuals differently, but common symptoms may include:
Emotional symptoms:
•	Persistent sadness
•	Feelings of hopelessness
•	Loss of interest or pleasure
•	Irritability
•	Feeling emotionally numb
•	Excessive guilt or worthlessness
Physical symptoms:
•	Fatigue or low energy
•	Changes in sleep
•	Changes in appetite or weight
•	Slowed movement or restlessness
•	Unexplained aches or pains
Thinking and concentration:
•	Difficulty concentrating
•	Poor memory
•	Indecisiveness
•	Negative thinking
•	Feeling overwhelmed
Symptoms generally persist for at least two weeks and interfere with daily functioning.
________________________________________
What's the difference between feeling sad and having depression?
Sadness is a normal human emotion that usually develops in response to a specific event and gradually improves with time.
Depression is different.
Symptoms often persist for weeks or months, may occur without an obvious cause, and significantly affect your ability to work, maintain relationships, care for yourself, or enjoy everyday life.
If your mood continues to interfere with daily functioning or feels difficult to overcome on your own, it may be time to seek a professional evaluation.
________________________________________
What causes depression?
Depression rarely has a single cause.
It usually develops because of a combination of factors, including:
•	Genetics and family history
•	Brain chemistry
•	Chronic stress
•	Trauma
•	Significant life changes
•	Hormonal changes
•	Chronic medical conditions
•	Sleep disorders
•	Certain medications
•	Social isolation
•	Grief or loss
Understanding these contributing factors helps us develop a treatment plan that addresses both symptoms and underlying causes.
________________________________________
Can depression cause physical symptoms?
Yes.
Depression is often associated with physical symptoms, including:
•	Fatigue
•	Low energy
•	Headaches
•	Body aches
•	Digestive symptoms
•	Sleep disturbances
•	Changes in appetite
•	Decreased motivation
Many people seek medical care for physical symptoms before realizing depression may be contributing.
Because mental and physical health are closely connected, we evaluate both during every psychiatric assessment.
________________________________________
What is Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia)?
Persistent Depressive Disorder, also known as dysthymia, is a form of chronic depression in which symptoms are generally less severe than major depression but last much longer—often for two years or more.
Individuals may describe feeling "down," "unmotivated," or "not themselves" for years without recognizing they have a treatable condition.
Because symptoms develop gradually, many people assume this is simply part of their personality or life circumstances.
Treatment can significantly improve quality of life.
________________________________________
What is Bipolar Disorder?
Bipolar Disorder is a mood disorder characterized by episodes of depression along with periods of unusually elevated, expansive, or irritable mood known as mania or hypomania.
During manic or hypomanic episodes, people may experience:
•	Increased energy
•	Decreased need for sleep
•	Racing thoughts
•	Increased confidence
•	Impulsivity
•	Risk-taking behaviors
•	Increased goal-directed activity
Not everyone with Bipolar Disorder experiences symptoms in the same way, which is why an accurate diagnosis is essential.
________________________________________
How is Bipolar Disorder different from depression?
Although depression is a major part of Bipolar Disorder, individuals with bipolar illness also experience periods of elevated mood or increased energy.
This distinction is important because treatments that work well for major depression may not always be appropriate for Bipolar Disorder.
A comprehensive psychiatric evaluation helps ensure the correct diagnosis and the safest, most effective treatment plan.
________________________________________
Can hormones affect depression?
Absolutely.
Hormonal fluctuations can significantly affect mood.
Some individuals experience depression related to:
•	Pregnancy
•	Postpartum changes
•	PMDD
•	Perimenopause
•	Menopause
•	Thyroid disorders
•	PCOS
•	Other endocrine conditions
Because these conditions may require a different treatment approach, we carefully evaluate hormonal and medical factors during every assessment.
________________________________________
Can medical conditions cause depression?
Yes.
Several medical conditions can contribute to depressive symptoms, including:
•	Thyroid disease
•	Diabetes
•	Chronic pain
•	Neurological disorders
•	Vitamin deficiencies
•	Autoimmune conditions
•	Sleep disorders
This is one reason a comprehensive psychiatric evaluation is so important. Addressing an underlying medical condition may improve emotional symptoms and overall well-being.
________________________________________
How are depression and mood disorders diagnosed?
Diagnosis begins with a thorough psychiatric evaluation.
Dr. Tandon reviews your symptoms, medical history, medications, family history, lifestyle, sleep, stressors, and any medical or hormonal factors that may be contributing to your mood changes.
Rather than focusing only on symptoms, we work to understand the complete picture so treatment recommendations are accurate and personalized.
________________________________________
How are depression and mood disorders treated?
Treatment depends on the underlying diagnosis, symptom severity, medical history, and your personal goals.
Your treatment plan may include:
•	Medication management
•	Supportive psychotherapy
•	Referral for ongoing therapy
•	Lifestyle recommendations
•	Sleep optimization
•	Stress management
•	Coordination with other healthcare providers
•	Education about your condition
Every treatment plan is individualized because every patient's experience is unique.
________________________________________
Can depression be treated without medication?
Yes.
Some individuals improve with psychotherapy, exercise, improved sleep, stress reduction, mindfulness practices, and lifestyle modifications.
Others benefit most from medication, especially when symptoms are more severe or have persisted despite non-medication approaches.
The decision to use medication is always collaborative and based on your individual circumstances and preferences.
________________________________________
What is burnout, and how is it different from depression?
Burnout is a state of emotional, mental, and physical exhaustion often related to prolonged workplace or caregiving stress.
Symptoms may include fatigue, reduced motivation, cynicism, decreased productivity, and feeling emotionally drained.
Although burnout and depression share many symptoms, they are not the same condition. Some people experience burnout alone, while others develop depression as a result of prolonged stress.
A psychiatric evaluation can help distinguish between the two and guide the most appropriate treatment.
________________________________________
Can depression affect memory and concentration?
Yes.
Many people with depression experience what is sometimes called "brain fog."
They may notice:
•	Difficulty concentrating
•	Poor memory
•	Slower thinking
•	Trouble making decisions
•	Reduced productivity
These symptoms often improve as depression is effectively treated.
________________________________________
Can depression return after treatment?
Unfortunately, it can.
Some people experience only one episode of depression, while others have recurring episodes throughout life.
Regular follow-up care, healthy lifestyle habits, psychotherapy, medication when appropriate, and early recognition of symptoms can significantly reduce the risk of relapse.
Our goal is not only to treat current symptoms but also to help prevent future episodes whenever possible.
________________________________________
When should I seek help for depression?
You don't have to wait until symptoms become severe.
Consider seeking an evaluation if:
•	Your mood has remained low for more than two weeks
•	You have lost interest in activities you once enjoyed
•	Your work or relationships are suffering
•	You feel emotionally exhausted
•	You are withdrawing from others
•	You are struggling to complete everyday tasks
•	You feel hopeless or overwhelmed
Early intervention often leads to better outcomes and can prevent symptoms from becoming more difficult to manage.
________________________________________
What if I'm having thoughts of harming myself?
If you are having thoughts of harming yourself or feel that you may be in immediate danger, this is a medical emergency.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department immediately. You can also call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline to speak with a trained crisis counselor at any time.
If your thoughts are not immediate or life-threatening but are becoming more frequent or concerning, please contact our office as soon as possible so we can help determine the safest next steps.
You do not have to face these feelings alone, and help is available.
________________________________________
How can Paramount Psychiatry help?
At Paramount Psychiatry, we recognize that depression and mood disorders affect every aspect of life—not just your emotions.
Dr. Tandon takes a thoughtful, whole-person approach to care, considering your medical history, hormonal health, sleep, stress, relationships, and life circumstances in addition to your symptoms. Whether you're experiencing depression for the first time, living with Bipolar Disorder, coping with persistent low mood, or struggling with burnout, our goal is to understand your unique experience and develop a treatment plan that helps you regain hope, improve daily functioning, and enhance your overall quality of life.
Healing is possible, and you don't have to navigate it alone.

Women's Mental Health & Hormone-Related:

A woman's mental health is influenced by
much more than emotions alone. Hormonal changes throughout life—including
menstruation, pregnancy, postpartum recovery, perimenopause, menopause, thyroid
disorders, and conditions such as Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)—can
significantly affect mood, anxiety, sleep, concentration, and overall emotional
well-being.

**What is Women's Mental Health?**

Women's Mental Health is a specialized area
of psychiatry that focuses on emotional and psychological well-being throughout
the different stages of a woman's life.

Hormonal changes can influence brain
chemistry, sleep, stress response, energy levels, concentration, and mood.
Because these changes often overlap with anxiety, depression, ADHD, thyroid
disorders, and other medical conditions, a comprehensive evaluation is
essential for making an accurate diagnosis and developing an effective
treatment plan.

Our goal is to understand the complete
picture—not simply treat individual symptoms.

---

**Why do hormones affect mental health?**

Hormones act as chemical messengers
throughout the body and have important effects on the brain.

Changes in estrogen, progesterone, thyroid
hormones, and other endocrine systems can influence neurotransmitters that
regulate mood, anxiety, sleep, motivation, memory, and emotional resilience.

For some women, these hormonal changes cause
only mild symptoms. For others, they may contribute to significant depression,
anxiety, irritability, panic attacks, insomnia, or difficulty concentrating.

Understanding these biological changes
allows us to provide more personalized and effective care.

---

**What conditions do you treat as part of
Women's Mental Health?**

Paramount Psychiatry evaluates and treats a

- Premenstrual      Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)
- Premenstrual      mood changes
- Pregnancy-related      mood and anxiety disorders
- Postpartum      depression
- Postpartum      anxiety
- Perimenopause
- Menopause
- Hormone-related      depression and anxiety
- Mood      changes associated with PCOS
